raw_text:
### Introduction and Epidemiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive and infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium [1]. Once considered rare, recent advances in diagnostic modalities have revealed CA to be an underdiagnosed and relatively common cause of heart failure [2, 3]. The two primary forms of CA are light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, arising from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia that produces monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains [4], and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), which involves the misfolding of the liver-synthesized transport protein transthyretin [5, 6]. ATTR can be further classified into wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), an age-related condition predominantly affecting older males, and hereditary or variant ATTR (ATTRv), caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the *TTR* gene [6, 7].

### Pathophysiology and Clinical Manifestations
The pathophysiology of CA involves mechanical disruption of the myocardial architecture by amyloid fibrils, leading to restrictive cardiomyopathy, severe diastolic dysfunction, and eventual systolic failure [1, 15]. In AL amyloidosis, circulating monoclonal light chains also exert direct cardiotoxic effects, contributing to a much more aggressive clinical course compared to ATTR [14, 20]. 

Clinically, CA typically presents as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), progressive dyspnea, and fatigue [11, 26]. Electrocardiography (ECG) often reveals low voltage or a pseudoinfarction pattern, creating a classic mismatch with the severe left ventricular wall thickening observed on echocardiography [5, 17]. Systemic "red-flag" symptoms, such as bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, and autonomic neuropathy, frequently precede cardiac symptoms by years, especially in patients with ATTR [6, 26].

### Diagnostic Advancements
The diagnostic paradigm for CA has evolved dramatically, enabling non-invasive diagnosis in many cases [3]. Echocardiography typically demonstrates concentric ventricular hypertrophy and a pathognomonic "apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain [5, 13]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides exquisite tissue characterization, showing diffuse late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) alongside markedly elevated native T1 times and extracellular volume (ECV) fraction [7, 27].

The diagnostic algorithm for ATTR has been revolutionized by bone-seeking radiotracers, such as technetium-99m-pyrophosphate ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-PYP) or technetium-99m-dicarboxydiphosphonate ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-DPD) [12, 18]. Grade 2 or 3 myocardial uptake on nuclear scintigraphy in the absence of a detectable monoclonal protein in serum or urine is 100% specific for ATTR, which obviates the need for endomyocardial biopsy [3, 13]. Crucially, screening for monoclonal proteins via serum/urine immunofixation and serum free light chain (sFLC) assays is mandatory in all suspected cases, as AL amyloidosis requires emergency oncological therapy [8, 28]. If a monoclonal protein is present, or if diagnostic ambiguity persists, a tissue biopsy stained with Congo red showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light remains the gold standard [1, 21]. Genetic sequencing of the *TTR* gene must follow an ATTR diagnosis to differentiate ATTRwt from ATTRv [22, 25].

### Prognosis and Risk Staging
Prognosis in CA is dictated by the amyloid subtype and the severity of cardiac involvement [14, 24]. In AL, risk stratification relies on Mayo Clinic staging using cardiac troponins, NT-proBNP, and free light chain levels [14, 24]. For ATTR, the Gillmore staging system utilizes NT-proBNP and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) [25]. Untreated AL has a grim prognosis, with survival often measured in months from the onset of heart failure, whereas ATTR exhibits a slower, but still relentlessly progressive, clinical course [11, 20].

### Therapeutic Strategies
The management of CA has transitioned from purely supportive care to highly effective, disease-modifying therapies [6, 16]. In AL amyloidosis, treatment is directed at suppressing the clonal plasma cell dyscrasia [28]. The landmark ANDROMEDA trial established the combination of daratumumab, bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone (Dara-CyBorD) as the first-line standard of care, achieving deep hematological and clinical responses [8, 23]. Autologous stem cell transplantation remains an option for highly selected eligible patients [28].

For ATTR, management focuses on TTR stabilization or gene silencing [6, 17]. Tafamidis, a small-molecule TTR stabilizer, was shown in the ATTR-ACT trial to significantly reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations, establishing it as the current standard of care [2, 19]. Gene silencers, such as patisiran (an siRNA) and inotersen (an antisense oligonucleotide), knock down hepatic TTR production and have demonstrated clinical efficacy in halting neuropathy progression in ATTRv [9, 10]. The recent APOLLO-B trial demonstrated that patisiran also improves functional capacity and quality of life in patients with ATTR cardiomyopathy [30]. Liver transplantation, historically used for ATTRv, is now rarely performed due to the success of these novel agents [29]. 

Supportive care focuses on careful fluid management with loop diuretics and aldosterone antagonists, whereas traditional heart failure medications like beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are often poorly tolerated or contraindicated [16, 22].

### Conclusion
The clinical approach to cardiac amyloidosis has been transformed by non-invasive diagnostic pathways and disease-modifying therapies that improve survival and quality of life [3, 17]. Early clinical recognition of "red flags" is essential to initiate timely treatment and arrest disease progression [6, 22].
